title: Wrong notes and a sudden song
work: Étude in E minor, Op. 25 No. 5
question: What changes when Chopin’s teasing semitone clashes open into a song?
intro: Chopin’s tune keeps catching on the note next door. Goldstein and Neeman turn from its quick semitone clashes to a slower E-major song, low in the piano. When the opening returns, the clipped chords sound mischievous again.

recordings.label: Edward Neeman, c. 2014
recordings.note: Neeman’s teacher Larry Sitsky wrote his First Piano Sonata for him; Neeman made its first recording.

recordings.label: Martha Goldstein
recordings.note: Goldstein’s Érard was built in Paris in 1851 and restored with its original hammers and action.

passages.label: The note next door
passages.note: Quick semitone clashes interrupt the tune; clipped chords and little hesitations keep the opening on its toes.

passages.label: A song in E major
passages.note: In E major, the left hand sings a broad melody while the right hand rolls upwards and downwards around it.

passages.label: The teasing tune returns
passages.note: The quick E-minor opening returns, with its short phrases and semitone nudges after the long central song.

sources.title: Mieczysław Tomaszewski, Chopin Institute — the scherzando opening, cello-like middle melody and return
Op. 25 No. 5 — semitone dissonances, E-major middle section and return
